game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is interesting, the UI is fantastic, but...

The writing doesn't work. Not to me, at least.

So the idea is, you're an anonymous member of the public working with a new program that's half google, half snooping software. You're assigned a case - the first one is about a bomb placed in a plaza, and thanks to surveillance cameras you're assigned to look up everything about a suspect. So far so good, right? There's the relevant question of whether it's right to spy on someone in the name of public safety, there's a mystery to solve...

But it falls apart. Your supervisor is all "she has a police record, let's snoop on her" and okay, good enough reason to investigate...her faux-facebook page, her faux-portfolio, news websites, etcetera. Except that none of these websites feel like they were ever used by real people, her facebook timeline feels bizarre, like she's a fascimile of a human being, and when you get to eavesdrop on her text messages with her boyfriend, again it feels false?

Everything is off, and not in a good way. And your supervisor is so ready to pin the entire case on her because she's joined an activist group that organizes protests against the surveillance state.

It's too on the nose, with writing that doesn't sell to me that I'm snooping on real people, with a wonky "this is taking place in real time" - but it's not, really, you only get to eavesdrop on people's text conversations when you unlock them, not when they happen - and it all just feels clumsy.

In a game that's only got its writing going for it, having a fantastically slick UI isn't going to keep me playing it. Which is a bummer! The questions this game is asking are relevant, and it's so slick and pretty to look at I want to dig into it! ... But sadly it's just not compelling.

Bummer.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Dig into the forums on this one before you purchase.  It's not quite the game description implies.   

As one person put it it's more of a "visual novel" where you play the untrusty narrator in an Orwellian future.  Great content and rich interface support that experience.   However if you're looking for the rabbit whole where you're investigating and shaping the lives of these "potential criminals" then this game misses that mark by not providing an organic sense of discovery to the player.  Most of the game is on rails, because it has to be, with so much content involved.

The creators put a lot of blood and treasure into this game and new content is coming out each week.  If you're looking to read a captivating story about a dark future ahead, then this game is for you (even more so after this week's election results).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
TL;DR: Don't bother, you're basically just a human web-crawler.

This game completely misses the point of what Orwellian infrastructure would look like in the first place and does everything in its power to not allow you any information at all. This game has no right to call itself Orwell, it has nothing to do with surveillance. Yea you have access to data, but the constant opinionated non-rational commentary by the "Adviser" undermines the whole of it. I can't of course claim the outcome wouldn't be the same in an actually Orwellian policy, but it sure as hell shouldn't look like this. In no way am I defending Orwellian values either, but their implementation here is.. well it isn't. It's just not there.
When choose information to be considered, the information changes between the point where you drag it from and the actual information recorded. 
The UI is unintuitive and very hard to navigate. The artificial load times don't help either, from both the gameplay loop and story-telling perspective, they make no sense.

Just to blow of some steam about how disappointed I am in this game, I'll address a couple reviews:

“Grabs the problem of how we balance our own liberty and our safety and turns it into a thrilling adventure.” 9/10 – Polygon
It does make a feeble attempt at tackling the problem of balancing safety and liberty, but fails miserably. Not only does it not represent what you could call Orwellian infrastructure, it doesn't even try. Access to information is limited and the information itself misinterpreted. Your "superior" is clearly opinionated, easily influenced and not of very high deductive capacity. Hardly a "thrilling adventure", the pace of the game is dictated by the game, not by the player. You can't move fast, despite the game making constant remarks about how you should. Nothing about this is thrilling, it's a very slow burner, except it isn't good. It's attempting to show flaws in Orwellian policies but fails to represent them, only showing flaws in its own design.

“A harrowing look into a reality where Big Brother is always watching” Rock Paper Shotgun
The only "harrowing" thing about this game is how it managed to get out of indev. The UI of this game is atrocious in both mechanical as well as logical sense. Mechanically navigating anywhere in this game is a pain in the bum, and the game punishes you every time you try to make more than 1 action per 10 seconds. The whole bit about conflicting data chunks is just stupid. First of all it should have a dating mechanism in the data collection software, which would prevent 90% of the data chunk conflicts in the first place. Secondly, why bother trying to pick one out of the 2 conflicting data points when all you're doing is presenting to someone who can clearly barely tie their own shoe-laces, much less decide outcomes for other people. I wouldn't let this "Adviser" choose the color of desktop background, much less my or anyone else's legal standing. Oh and did I mention: You can't go back on whatever the "Adviser" was saying either, so tough luck if you wanted to submit 2 pieces of information and started navigating before you can notice the Adviser popping up on screen, immediately skipping possibly vital dialog.

“In an age where so much personal information is willingly released by so many, Orwell brilliantly explores the implications of this data being misinterpreted.” 8/10 – GameSpot
This. That's the exact problem with the game, there isn't supposed to be an interpretation to be done in the first place. At the start of the game, you're presented with the job of a data-gatherer. It's not up to you to interpret this data and neither should it be up to the "Adviser". Not just because his brain activity matches that of a fork, but because he simply does not have all the data. Neither does the player, nobody does. Once the information is conclusive all on it's own and only then should there be an attempt at interpretation. It's a simple rational analysis up until then. Or at least it should've been. Instead the game constantly pedals it's own point with forced story-telling.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game could have been good, and the story is compelling to a certain extent. You can tell there is something that isn't being said that you can't find, and it makes it all the more important to find it. But thats where the fun stops, and where the frustration begins.

Probably the most aggrivating thing about this game is the inability to directly say what information you extract should mean. Instead you effectively hand over little quips of information to a conspiricy theorist and then wonder how that information is going to be used. Probably the biggest instance of this is when you are going to arrest a certain character, you get into a certain call. You learn that she is on the move, and has a hand gun. You submit that she has a gun and suddenly you basicaly called the fekin army down on her and she dies, when all evidence before then would suggest that going Riot-shields fer days would have been the correct move.

Also when handed "Contradicting evidence", often times the information isn't contradicting, but should have been able to be combined to paint something that would have been more conductive to profiling the person in question. Things like where the suspect lives now and previously, which both could be noted and later on used to help track down said person.

The lack of proper notes is, while not entirely nessisary for the set up of the game, probably a bad decision. Notes could have been used to snip articles with evidence that your unsure of how to use at the present moment and would have helped during the "Scrolling sections" disguised as Texts and calls. While you can scroll up during any moment of these, being able to hold out on certain information for a better time would have helped immensely.

So all in all, a great premise and the story works, execution worked about as well as alcohol and fire.

I've seen free games on Kongregate that are longer to finish than this game. Also, it's another of these incompleted games that comes into chapters... I mean come on! This ain't a graphic-based game, surely you can publish a complete game... it's just text damnit! I know games in the 1980s that were deeper than this!

Where is the gaming industry heading anyways with such tiny games? Make this thing free. If I can get bigger better games for free, why should I pay for this?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a game that I have mixed feeling about. While I did enjoy the game, I also want to clarify that there is certainly more than one issue with the game that makes me want to not recommend it.

The gameplay boils down to one and only one mechanic. Being able to drag selected text into a profile which affects the story. You need to bounce between internet pages, phone-call logs, and a few other forms of data to find keywords and important text to upload. Depending on what you upload, what the government believes and what happens to the person(s) involved changes. Do you portray a spoiled brat as a terrorist? An old man as a kind teacher. You decide what information they've put online defines them, very literally. 

The issues I have with this is as such: 
[olist]
    [*]Choices don't ultimately matter.
    [*]It is painfully short.
    [*]A lack of any audio design.
[/olist]

From top to bottom, the linearity of the game. Despite being able to chose what information does or doesn't get uploaded, a lot (and I do mean a LOT) of events will happen regardless of your actions. The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence.

Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much.

Lastly, the audio design. As previously mentioned, there is little to no audio in this game. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game.

The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more.

I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

The game literally says in it's description: "But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences." However, despite this, the only things my choices ended up affecting were the achievements. And spoiler alert: [spoiler] You can get any of the three endings no matter what choices you made in previous episodes. [/spoiler] Sure, on a superficial surface level your choices have consequences, but these "consequences" never actually impact your story or gameplay expericence. Onto the next, the length. You may see me having 7.5 hours and tell me "Oh well 7.5 hours in NOT a short game!" You'd be right. Except Orwell is not 7.5 hours long, it is 3 hours long at most and 2 hours long at it's shortest. The only reason I have more than 3 hours of playtime is because I went back to get all of the achievements, which is also why i know how little your choices affect the story. I've seen all the endings, seen the affect of almost all of the choices, and even then with some time spent idle I was able to see 99% of this game's offerings in under 8 hours. This isn't inherently bad, but Orwell has little to no gameplay, audio design, or anything. It's just an on rails story, and for it to be that short for a $10 USD price tag is a little much. You have 3 music tracks, the main menu theme, the basic ambient theme and a more intense theme for when things "get serious." Outside of the music, you might have a few computer beeps or a quick musical tone at random points, but they're so spread out that a majority of your time is spent with almost nothing going into your ears. You can't hear people on their phone calls, your boss can't speak to you, there are no audio transcripts. It is the most barebones audio design I've seen in a story driven game. The only really good thing I'd argue in favor of is the art style. It is a fractal/cubism artstyle that absolutely draws you in. The issue is that this art style is not the primary focus, instead that focus is on a painfully bland UI. If you look at the screenshots on the store page, you see that profile tab on the right, your bar up top and the righthand screen? That is 90% of the game. Just looking at those screens It could've been so much more. I really like the idea of Orwell, an Orwellian (pun not intended) dystopia with a spying government and terrorist plots. The thing that makes me not like it though is literally everything else about it. And that is the problem.

review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish there were a rating between recommended and not recommended. Like a 'Eh, maybe?' option.  This game is very well designed with a great UI and intuitive progression. You do make some decisions and those decisions do have a pretty big impact on the story, but that is also where the bulk of my criticism comes from.

The decisions that make a huge difference feel incredibly arbitrary, so instead of feeling like you're investigating and making decisions, it feels like a game of guessing what the *developers* want you to do. It also railroads you into things I don't agree with and wouldn't choose to do, but if you don't do them you get stuck or really bad things happen. The guy you interact with (your point of contact) is very volatile and makes weirdly intense decisions off of very limited information, which can entirely screw up your game if you're going for the best results for everyone involved and it can be really hard to tell when he's going to do that. 

Initially I tried to play cautiously, withholding information I felt could be abused, and that ended up with people dying. So I quit where I was and restarted the whole game (boring, because this game is not very replayable) and had to try a few times before I figured out exactly what was causing the issue. Then I thought I better understood the game so I continued, only to find that I gave *too much* information to them which resulted in more deaths. 

It just doesn't feel like a game where the goal is about making the *best* decisions, it feels like a game where the goal is making whatever decisions the devs want you to make, and that's too much random guesswork to be fun for me. I stopped playing after Chapter 2 because I was tired of trying to read their minds.

review_text_raw:
I hesitated before giving the thumb down to a game which is not completely bad, but definitely not for everyone.
The game basically plays like a visual story where you have to grab (drag  & drop more exactly) chunks of data to the left of the screen on the right character, the interface is not perfect (no right clicking to add intel faster, some back buttons are just visuals). The game is SLOW and a bit boring if you play in one go, no way to speed up text, no voice acting, forces you to wait on a few occasions. 
The writing isn't bad but characters lack personnality (bit shallow, not enough background), the game forces you to go one way and lacks some imaginative gameplay (older games would have make you work with visual clues, make interrogation yourself but Orwell keeps making you reading text). The problem is that it plays like a slow VN where you have to constantly look for the next button without any way to speed things up. 
It's not overly long but it feels long and the whole debate it's supposed to bring up falls a bit flat, also you can guess the "responsible person" before the end as soon as some intel is revealed. 
The game offers several ends but does not warn you before making the final choice (it did force you to watch a wall of text on an ugly colored screen before though) and would force you to replay from scratch to make another choice.

Don't mistaken me, those who are in for a lengthy text experience set in the modern world with text centered spying are in for a treat but it's definitely not for everyone.

review_text_raw:
There really should be a "maybe" option for steam reviews... Orwell is a decent game, just not the kind of game that is engaging for me.

Orwell is more a graphic adventure game rather than the espionage game it was advertised as. If you like Life is Strange, you'd probably like Orwell. 
Sadly this is not my cup of tea. I want to actually think and *play* a game. If I want a story I'd watch a movie or a let's play... The story had to be deeper than this for me to be interested.

The good:
Orwell did a good job at designing the user interface. It's beautiful, functional, and believable. The artstyle is unique and pleasing to the eye.
You'd find that despite the handholding, you will have to make choices that will have separate story outcomes. Some choices are more "right" than others, There're be hints in the game to help you make the right choice, so the choices are at least not just random.

The bad:
However, just like the other reviewers had pointed out, the articles and character profiles are too simplistic, it doesn't feel "real" enough. This design choice is understandable since adding fluff and pointless information just for the sake of making the sites "real" doesn't help with immersion either. What would help with immersion is the compelling content; which I find sadly lacking here... I find myself just skimming through for highlights. It's too much hand-holding for my taste. Really, they could have made it so much better by just making the relevant text unhighlighted so we have to actually spend effort reading and playing the game as "intended".

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
It's a nice concept but it falls short in execution.
The game is way too short. I was done in about 5 hours, and I had restarted in the first chapter because I didn't like the portrait I chose for my character (no way to edit this after character creation).

It's too linear. You are steered down a very narrow path of choices. It's like one of those point and click adventures that only goes in one direction. I thought the game would be open with some freedom, but you're locked into specific paths to progress the game.

The game makes no usage of the camera and facial recognition tech you see in the trailers. It's all a desktop themed UI where you browse web pages, watch text chat between 3rd parties, and look at people's computers starting with their desktop.

The story itself is interesting, but doesn't distract you from the rails the game chugs along on. For $10, I expected something more then 5 hours of following mouse clicks.

It can drag, and the moral dilemmas lose punch when the moment-to-moment experience is so dry and repetitive. Not much in the way of challenge or variety either.If you must play it, stick to PC where it runs fine and the mouse and keyboard setup suits the desktop-sim style. Overall though, not for me. 4/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
While I appreciate the game's ideas, its theme and story, it is sadly a heavily scripted game. 

I wasn't planning on buying the game any time soon but decided to give it a go while it was free. I can't say I didn't enjoy it.
The presentation and the interface are great but it's the account creation single-handedly managed to freak me out, questioning what was I putting myself into. So right there, they nailed the art direction, period

However, the plot felt really cheesy while the whole story lasts five days-ish ... Which is kind of ridiculous with such a big-brother-thing going on. Nearly every character was 2Dimensional (though Nina really hits hard on the feels, man). The web of connection between all characters at the bottom left corner of the screen looks cool but is sadly useless... (Unless the player could've been able to enlarge said screen and/or add more branches.
Would've been even awesomer, plot-wise, if the player could've manipulated the branches on that web...)
It's really deceiving when it is advertised that you spy on npc's lives when all you do really is read a lot about their stuff until the game's mechanic highlights the script for you. Even when highlighting was not enough, dramatic music kicks in for added wink, wink, nodge, nodge...

I keep finding more and more things to pick at the more I write about/review this game... 

It's a cool idea, to flip the table, to be with the ''bad'' guys, to sit on big brother's lap (or, in this case Big Data), that's for sure... But the execution as a video game, it's not nearly as profound as its intentions. It feels like it was made during a GameJam.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought Orwell (on sale) expecting a sort of 1984 screens, eyes, with wiretaps everywhere. What I got was a message pop up game with a pretty compelling story. In that sentence, I just described the whole review. If you didn't get it - keep reading!

They say it's wrong to assume, and definitely after playing this, it's wrong to make assumptions sometimes. If there is a demo available, try it! This one didn't have it, and it was on sale - so I went for it. The [b]story[/b] is pretty good and well thought out, and has some serious twists and turns as it progresses. The characters are interesting and the game does a good job to keep the player guessing. The [b]gameplay[/b] revolves around making decisions on what to upload to "Orwell" (or the computer that connects all the dots) to decide the fate of the citizens that are being investigated. Basically. a text-rich game. Once a decision is made things get set in motion, very quick. During a specific period in the game I had the habit of uploading everything... just be careful what is deemed important! Someone may wrongly get arrested. 

The [b]visuals and graphics[/b] are very easy on the eyes. However, if you're someone who likes when the screen changes every once in a while, this might not totally be up your alley. The game consists of three or so main screens. The first is a headline type screen. This screen lets the player browse the web for interesting information they may come across. The second screen allows the player (working for Orwell) to listen in on live conversations or messages. The third screen is a computer hacking screen in which the player has access to a suspects computer. The game does a good progression to introducing the player to what is going on. The [b]sounds and music[/b] are pretty decent. There are moments in the game where the music will slam and something dramatic will happen. The sounds are alright and there is no live voice to the characters. I imagine being a small developper that can be hard to do, but the text does a decent job delivering a story. I'm not a text sort of gamer (my friend bought me Disco Elysium, I'm sure it's great, but just don't have the patience to play it), this game did catch my attention for a while though.

Why the negative review? If I had to warn my past self, I would advise my past self not to buy it. It's an awesome story, there are cool things that happen, but I feel indifferent to the game. I went down a mystery and I was put on the edge. Not enough for me to really like the game. If you like text based games and something that's a little different on Steam, or even mystery, decisions, and consequences... and especially if this game is on sale, I'd say definitely give it a shot. For me, I had a little fun. That's about it. It is sort of similar to Papers Please; Orwell is a little more linear to one story line. There are branches, but limited. The ending though, was definitely, as some would say, dope.  

This game has a story with a real lesson for the future. Would be interesting to see a new version of this game with more options and new tools to use.

review_text_raw:
TL;DR: If you want to be a pedantic bureaucrat, play "Papers, please" instead.


Long story:

This can be an exciting game if you're not one who likes nitpicking. However, if you do (which is maybe why you're drawn to it in the first place), you will pull some hairs out in rage and discontent.

The game focuses on monitoring an increasing set of data (news, websites, chat logs, phone calls etc) to look for leads in a specific case on which the game is built up. Whatever the game means is relevant will be highlighted, and you'll have the choice to either submit it to the investigators or ignore it. The info will also be rewritten, i.e. concentrated to what the game thinks it means.

This poses two problems - 1) the data YOU might think is highly relevant or more relevant isn't highlighted. And 2) the data you find may not be the data that will be submitted. For example, someone SUGGESTS to someone else that they do something. If you submit it, it's altered to say that the person PLANNED it. When talking about a crime that may or may not have occurred, this is a very important difference. Casually suggesting something and planning it is not the same. Everything you submit will be used by the police to decide which actions to take, so you might want to ignore that piece of info then.. if you can (explained further down).

review_text_raw:
Orwell does one thing very well: it accurately simulates the tedium inherent in most government jobs. If you ever wanted to know what it's like to work at the DMV or IRS, Orwell is your game. The simplistic click-and-drag gameplay might have been mitigated by an interesting story or characters, but Orwell's plot is boilerplate paranoia fiction delivered in screen after screen of dull exposition. The puzzle design vacillates between the extremes of baffingly obtuse and blaringly obvious. At several points, I found myself simply clicking through every single screen and selecting every random bit of data I could simply to progress the story.

On the plus side, the ambient soundtrack is pleasant and includes the occasional dramatic sting to highlight twists in the storyline. The Orwell UI is clean and easy to navigate. I also think that the developers had the best of intentions to create a game that grapples with the rise of the surveillance state in modern societies.

Unfortunately, good intentions don't trump bad game design. Stay away from Borewell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell S1 is an Alternate Reality Game condensed into a single program. Big Brother deals with terrorists, and it tries to turn into a chicken and egg situation. Gameplay consists of filing clips off a mock web into a police social graph, or not. Occasionally you have to read more to resolve contradictions, which is the high point of the experience, along with a midgame sequence I shan't spoil. 

Its UI is pretty but remarkably unrefined. The keyboard shortcuts and wheel scrolling you've come to expect from browsers seem absent. The social graph will let nodes partially overlap and poorly arranges them, but you can't actually manually fix it. The base gameplay loop is spot juicy clipping on the right, open the relevant person's file on the left, then drag clipping into profile. Aliases are occasionally used, but for the vast majority of cases it's obvious who the clip is about, so the rigmarole could have been boiled down to a click. Some views overlap elements in a way the rest of the game doesn't, and dealing with that is awkward.

The finale of Season 1 came remarkably abruptly for me (about 80% too early in fact); this accidental completion meant I didn't get to deal with all as I intended.

Storywise, it works. There's a few polished plot twists and turns, and character color for several members of the cast, and the story arc goes exactly where you expect it to from the get go. It's neither subtle nor [i]Sledge Hammer![/i] in its didactisism, which is good because I expect there's few potential customers who need the lecture. The best addition was the seemingly frivolous choice of player profile picture, which got me to role play a bit an elderly, seen-it-all lady.

I estimate about 4 hours of my playtime was the main arc, and then about one more of reading the weather forecasts and such.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You is a thought-provoking game that successfully delves into the complex world of surveillance and privacy, raising numerous ethical questions and dilemmas. Its core premise, which involves taking on the role of a government operative monitoring citizens' digital lives, is both innovative and unsettling. It challenges players to balance national security with personal privacy, making every decision carry significant weight and moral ambiguity.

Gameplay Mechanics

The mechanics are straightforward, primarily revolving around reading through documents, chat logs, and social media posts to piece together clues about potential threats. While this simplicity makes the game accessible, it can also lead to a repetitive and tedious experience. The process of sifting through information often lacks variety, and the gameplay can become monotonous over time. Moreover, the game's interface, although intuitive, sometimes suffers from minor bugs that can force you to reload the Game. There are also some minor instances where progression is unclear, leaving players uncertain about their next steps.

Narrative and Storytelling

One of the strengths of Orwell lies in its narrative, which includes several compelling plot twists that keep the player engaged. The story explores themes of power, trust, and the consequences of unchecked surveillance, offering moments of genuine intrigue and suspense. However, despite these high points, the overall plot can feel somewhat bland and unremarkable by the conclusion. The characters, while initially interesting, sometimes lack depth, and the story does not always capitalize on its potential to deliver a truly memorable experience.

Ethical Themes and Impact

Where Orwell truly shines is in its exploration of ethical issues. The game does not shy away from presenting the moral complexities of surveillance, forcing players to confront the impact of their actions on individuals' lives. This aspect of the game is its most compelling feature, prompting players to reflect on real-world implications and the delicate balance between security and privacy.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't ever write reviews, but I have an overwhelming urge to say what's on my mind. With no one to rant to, I'll just use this as an outlet (and it'll provide good reference material when i come back in a couple years to figure out why i didn't like this game).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Gameplay / Mechanics[/b]

the game is simple. you parse information for the important bits and then drag and drop that information into people's profiles. the game pre-selects certain segments of text and highlights them for you and then gives you the choice of determining whether it's important or true enough to include in their file. and therein lies the problem. you're given almost no autonomy, making the game less engaging. 99% of the time, you just scroll through articles and web pages looking for the highlighted text and then dragging and dropping it. there's no limit to how much data i can gather, so i don't have to think about whether this information is important enough to include and just include it anyway. and any false information that might be misleading is made extremely obvious. like when someone lists their address as "the interwebs". if there's any data that conflicts with another piece of data, it's highlighted in yellow and presented to you as a choice. you can only choose one of these to include in their file and your decision will effect the outcome (or so i assume, having not played the game more than once). these are the more engaging parts of the game as it forces me to analyze both data chunks' context and make a real decision. but each of these moments are fleeting and within a handful of seconds, i'm back to mindlessly scrolling through files again. there's one moment in the game that breaks this trend. they limit the amount of information you can include and that was the best part of the game. i actually had to sit down and read everything before figuring out what parts i thought were important. for the first time, i actually felt immersed in this world and my role in it. that's how i think the whole game should have been. instead, i was given brainless and mundane tasks, leaving me twiddling my thumbs for the majority of the game.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Story[/b]

the story is actually pretty good. the mystery is slowly unraveled as you discover more information and you're given a few twists and turns to keep you on your toes. the story is paced well, nothing feels rushed or pedantically slow and takes its own time to develop its characters and world. the characters feel real. a couple fall to mere caricatures, but the game does well at representing these characters in more than one dimension. take for example nina, a character who at first seems like an extremist but is slowly revealed to be a single mother just trying to make ends meet by doing odd jobs. the only character that irritated me was your supervisor. every time you select a piece of information, he [i]has to[/i] comment on it in some way. he either made comments that don't matter and just made me roll my eyes (like when one character said they didn't like the government and your supervisor [i]just had to say[/i] "we don't like you either"). or he recapped [i]exactly[/i] what that data chunk said. or he told you something that was already extremely obvious (like when you find out that goldfels is already dead, he says "that means he couldn't be behind the bombings and someone is impersonating him". no duh). so when he gets targeted, i don't feel a whole lot of sympathy for him. 

i do not, however, like how the story is presented. the game consciously trades its gameplay for its narrative. you start to feel like less of an investigator trying to solve a mystery and more like a disneyland park goer on the [i]it's a a small world[/i] ride. you take a backseat and just watch what happens. contrast this to [i]Firewatch[/i], a similarly narrative driven game. it's mechanics are also extremely basic and boils down to a walking simulator game, but it delivers its story masterfully and makes you feel like [i]you[/i] are uncovering everything instead of everything being spat at you (like orwell does).

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Main Message[/b]

the game's main focus is to postulate the question, "should you trade privacy for security?" to which it answers "no". you take the role of what is essentially the thought police from george orwell's [i]1984[/i] and the game attempts to show you the inherent flaw of this. the end of the game breaks the fourth wall and speaks to you directly, asking you if what you've been doing is really okay. if spying on people is ethical or not, then puts the power in your hands. you can either expose the people you've been spying on this whole time or expose your boss. the problem is, the game never once makes me feel guilty or wrong or disgusted for having spied on these people's lives. in fact, it actively makes us feel justified for it. i stopped a bomb from going off in the biggest mall in the city. and when it came time to make that big decision in the end, of course i chose to expose this "thought" group because they rigged bombs and killed innocents. the game never addresses the morality of all of this and never makes me feel like i've overstepped my boundaries and question my actions. 

imagine this, as i'm going through a suspect's files (bob), i stumble upon bank statements that shows regular large-sum withdrawals. in some private conversations with his wife, he mentions having to take business trips, but his company's official records never mention any. we discover that he has a second phone with which he only contacts one person. the whole thing seems really shady and we have text messages of them planning to meet at the plaza an hour before the explosion, mentioning that he'll bring "the money". we get word that there's going to be another bombing within the hour. with the pressure mounting, we send in the police to intervene in the bob's next meeting and arrest them. during the interrogation, the bomb goes off. we find out that the bob's relation to his "contact" is a woman with which he had a one night fling and together had a baby, despite already having a family. they've been meeting together secretly so he can act as a stand-in father and support the them financially. bob loves his wife and kids and recognizes that he made a big mistake and is just trying to do his best in this crazy world. he has a responsibility to both his wife and his "contact". then sometime later (perhaps a couple chapters) we read a news article that says bob killed himself, detailing the events of his affair and how his wife divorced him. imagine how gut-wrenching that would be. to know that we ruined a guy's life because of what we did. by the end of the game, when we're asked whether or not what we did was right, that thought would would weigh heavy on my mind.

the game ends with an exposition based on your choices. in my case, the thought group is arrested and orwell is seeing full funding and support. it then has us start a profile on our own character like we've been doing all game, showing that we're also being spied on without our notice. i feel like this was supposed to be a punch to the gut, an immediate eye-opener, but it didn't do much for me. it would've been a lot more effective if it could pull information from my OS or my steam account and fill in the blanks with my real name, date of birth, email, etc. that would feel creepy and make my skin crawl a bit.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Orwell was a missed opportunity. it had a lot of potential to address contemporary issues with the ever-real presence of a "big brother" type figure spying on us even now. but the game falls flat and fails to gain my sympathy. the game feels like it was written by a 16 year old who just read [i]1984[/i] and circle-jerks how "deep" it is.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Painfully linear story telling. The choices in the game aren't really moral dilemmas on your part, it's a matter of trying to guess if the vague phrasing about a character's behavior is intentionally loaded with meaning or just bad writing within the game. There is almost zero re-play value and while it is 'pretty' it's very limited in terms of choices and interactive activity. If the game doesn't want you clicking on a certain item, it just sends you through a series of loops of graphics, which can also be confusing at the start of the game when you're trying to figure out what matters and what will change throughout the 'day' in the investigation. The interface, while accurate, really does remind you of your work computer. That's... not a compliment.

Some of the interesting questions this game briefly poses never get answered - including fleshing out details of certain characters you have compromising information on. In reality, you're not engaging with 90% of the text it tries to force-feed you. You're just searching for highlighted blurbs to obediently click and pass to the next marker. It's disappointing because it could have been so much more.

review_text_raw:
If i could have had data on the bombings (Type, Size, Distance), rewatch camera footage aswell as use the data collected through the investigations into the possible suspects, i could perhaps recommend this game, but you can't.
All you do is slowly scroll through news pages and conversations and piece together information while trying to avoid giving too much or too little information so the suspect you want to interrogate doesn't get off scott free (due to an awful interrogation) or shot.

Symes is the definition of idiot, supplying him with too little information may mean he interrogates even worse than he already does, while giving him too much will have him fly off the handle and order the team to shoot your best lead.

Sure, it's realistic if you believe everyone in law enforcement is as inept as he is.


Besides that i find scrolling through pages and conversations irritatingly slow, and i've been unable to speed it up.




Free, sure give it a whirl, but it's tiresome rather than thought-provoking.

Promising start, I'll keep an eye on this developer for sure but when it comes to Orwell I cannot give it more than a 5/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I do not recommend this game. Here's why.
First of all - it's boring. It really is. Gameplay-wise it offers just web browsing, reading stuff and clicking. Telltale's games do not offer much in gameplay, but at least you can watch pretty nice visuals and be engaged in the story. Here you just click and browse. Click and browse. And then browse and click a bit more. When I want to read (and I love reading) I read books, not games.
Second thing - visuals. Yes, the game's style and interface are aesthetically pleasing. But... first developers show lack of any effort to make the game rich in gameplay, then do the same with graphics. Yes they use nice colors. Yes the font is elegant. But it's easy to see how it was designed to be made quickly and effortlessly with those simple vectors. Perfect square on plain background is also aesthetically pleasant, but it doesn't show any craftsmanship. And yes, the art style is not crucial for game to be good. But it helps. Especially when game lacks in other areas.
And finally - the story itself. Game puts in you in the shoes of government worker. And it feels like work to play this game. And what kind of work is that? Spying on people and playing a god. Nothing to be proud of. Looks like you're the part of totalitarian machine, aimed at controlling the people. Taken straight from the Orwell's "Year 1984". Which is not necessarily a bad idea, but... the people you spy on are as obnoxious as your job and character you play. So which side developers really take? It looked like whether the game will try to convey I am doing something good, or those terrorist I'm trying to catch are "good" - I will be very, very disappointed. The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.
